card.tagline: Ritual dance of the Basarwa people marking life stages and healing in Botswana
card.profile: Tsutsube is a ritual dance and music tradition of the Basarwa (San) people in Botswana, originally centered in the Ghanzi and Kgalagadi regions. It is performed in four distinct stages: first kill, puberty, marriage, and trance, with the trance stage used for healing and spiritual engagement. The dance has spread across Botswana and into parts of South Africa’s North West province.
card.insight: Tsutsube unfolds in four ritual stages—first kill, puberty, marriage, and trance—each marking a vital community rite among Botswana’s Basarwa.

card.profile_long: Tsutsube is a traditional dance and music practice of the Basarwa, also known as the San people, indigenous to Botswana. It originated primarily in the Ghanzi and Kgalagadi regions but has since expanded to most parts of Botswana and even some areas of the North West province of South Africa. The dance is deeply ritualistic and performed in four defined categories or stages, each corresponding to significant life events or spiritual functions within the community. The first stage, known as the first kill, is a rite of passage for boys marking their transition into manhood. The puberty stage similarly marks the coming of age, while the marriage stage celebrates union and community bonds. The trance stage is distinct in its purpose, serving as a healing ritual where dancers enter trance states to engage with ancestral spirits, facilitating spiritual and physical healing. Tsutsube’s music and dance are inseparable, with rhythmic patterns and movements that support the ritual’s intent. While the exact musical instruments and choreographic details are not described in the sources, the dance’s importance as a living tradition among the Basarwa is clear. Tsutsube exemplifies how dance functions as a social and spiritual practice, preserving cultural identity and community cohesion. The spread of Tsutsube beyond its original regions reflects both the resilience and adaptability of Basarwa cultural expressions in contemporary Southern Africa.

claims.text: Tsutsube is a traditional dance and accompanying music in Botswana which is practiced by Basarwa or San people.
Tsutsube is performed in four ritualistic categories or stages which are the first kill, puberty, marriage and trance.
The first kill was for males or boys, and trance dance was for healing purposes to engage ancestors spirits.
Tsutsube was originally a dance genre that was associated with the Ghanzi and the Kgalagadi regions.
It has now spread around most parts of the country and some areas parts of the North West province of South Africa.
Tsutsube is part of the Southern African folk music and African folk dance traditions.
